content: Aspirin and dipyridamole are medications that work together as platelet aggregation inhibitors. They are FDA-approved for reducing the risk of stroke in patients who have experienced transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) or completed ischemic strokes caused by thrombosis. The combination of these drugs is not interchangeable with their individual components. The recommended adult dosage is one capsule taken orally twice daily, once in the morning and once in the evening. Capsules should be swallowed whole without chewing and can be taken with or without food. If intolerable headaches occur during initial treatment, the regimen may be adjusted to one capsule at bedtime and low-dose aspirin in the morning. However, patients should return to the standard regimen as soon as possible, typically within one week, as there is no outcome data supporting the adjusted regimen. Common adverse reactions include abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, and joint pain (arthralgia). Aspirin and dipyridamole are contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to any of the product components. Aspirin is also contraindicated in individuals with allergies to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and in those with the syndrome of asthma, rhinitis, and nasal polyps, as it may cause severe urticaria, angioedema, or bronchospasm. Aspirin should not be used in children or teenagers with viral infections due to the risk of Reye syndrome. Warnings include the potential for hypersensitivity reactions, bleeding risks, and the need to avoid aspirin in patients with severe hepatic or renal dysfunction. Aspirin and dipyridamole should be used cautiously in nursing mothers, as both drugs are excreted in human milk. The safety and effectiveness of this combination in pediatric patients have not been established, and its use in this population is not recommended. In clinical trials, such as the European Stroke Prevention Study-2 (ESPS-2), the combination of aspirin and dipyridamole demonstrated efficacy in reducing the risk of stroke. However, headache was a notable adverse effect, particularly during the first month of treatment. Other adverse reactions observed in less than 1% of patients included allergic reactions, dizziness, hypotension, gastrointestinal issues, and hearing disturbances like tinnitus. Drug interactions are significant with this combination. Dipyridamole can increase the cardiovascular effects of adenosine, and aspirin may diminish the effects of ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers. Concurrent use with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or NSAIDs increases the risk of bleeding. Aspirin can also interact with drugs like methotrexate, phenytoin, and valproic acid, potentially leading to toxicity or altered drug levels. In cases of overdose, symptoms are typically dominated by dipyridamole toxicity, including flushing, dizziness, and hypotension. Salicylate toxicity from aspirin may also occur, with early signs such as tinnitus and severe cases leading to hyperthermia and hypovolemia. Treatment involves supportive care, gastric lavage, activated charcoal, and correction of acid-base imbalances. Dialysis may be required for salicylate overdose, but it is not effective for dipyridamole due to its high protein binding. Pharmacologically, the antithrombotic action of this combination results from the additive antiplatelet effects of dipyridamole and aspirin. Dipyridamole inhibits phosphodiesterase and increases cyclic GMP levels, while aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase, reducing thromboxane A2 production. The pharmacokinetics of the two drugs are not significantly altered when co-administered. Aspirin and dipyridamole capsules contain 200 mg of extended-release dipyridamole and 25 mg of immediate-release aspirin. The inactive ingredients include acacia, lactose monohydrate, and titanium dioxide, among others. The capsule shell contains gelatin and iron oxides. In nonclinical studies, there was no evidence of carcinogenicity or mutagenicity with dipyridamole. However, aspirin alone has been associated with chromosomal aberrations in cultured human fibroblasts. The effects of the combination on fertility and reproductive performance have not been evaluated.
